title: auth-service CPU saturation from token validation hot loop
summary: CPU on auth-service jumped from a ~30% baseline to above 90% within two sample intervals and stayed pinned for 50 minutes.
root_cause: A deploy shipped a JWT validation path that re-parsed the signing key on every request instead of using the cached key. The parse is CPU-bound, so cost scaled linearly with request rate.
evidence: cpu_usage step change with no matching rise in request_rate; ERROR logs showed 'unhandled exception in request handler: TimeoutError' as requests queued behind the busy event loop.
resolution: Rolled back the deploy and restored the signing-key cache. CPU returned to baseline within one sample interval.
lesson: A CPU step change that is NOT accompanied by a request_rate rise points at work-per-request, not traffic.

title: payment-gateway latency drift from connection pool leak
summary: p50 latency on payment-gateway rose steadily from 50ms to about 90ms over twelve hours with no step change.
root_cause: A code path returned early on a validation failure without releasing its database connection. The pool drained slowly, so each request spent longer waiting for a free connection.
evidence: Monotonic latency ramp; WARN logs 'connection pool at N/64 in use, above soft limit' increasing in frequency across the window; ERROR logs 'failed to acquire database connection' appearing near the end.
resolution: Patched the early-return path to release the connection in a finally block; restarted the pool.
lesson: A slow monotonic ramp with rising pool-utilisation warnings is a leak, not load. Threshold alerts miss it because no single point is anomalous.

title: Correlated CPU rise across auth-service and user-profile from shared cache eviction
summary: Both auth-service and user-profile showed a small (~8%) CPU rise in the same two-hour window. Neither breached a single-service alert threshold.
root_cause: A shared Redis cluster hit its maxmemory limit and began evicting keys. Both services fell back to recomputing what they used to read from cache.
evidence: The rise was simultaneous and near-identical in magnitude on two services that share no code; each service alone looked like noise. Only the cross-service view made it visible.
resolution: Raised the cache memory limit and added an eviction-rate alert on the shared cluster.
lesson: Simultaneous small rises across unrelated services almost always mean a shared dependency. Per-service detectors are structurally blind to this.

title: payment-gateway error_rate spike from expired downstream TLS certificate
summary: error_rate went from under 1% to 34% instantly at 00:00 UTC and stayed flat until the certificate was replaced.
root_cause: The TLS certificate for the downstream billing-api expired exactly at midnight UTC. Every outbound call failed handshake.
evidence: Perfectly square error_rate step aligned to a round clock boundary; ERROR logs 'upstream timeout after Nms calling billing-api' dominating the window; latency rose because of handshake retries.
resolution: Replaced the certificate and added expiry monitoring at 30/14/7 days.
lesson: A square-edged change aligned to a round clock time is almost never organic — look for scheduled expiry, cron, or a config rollout.

title: user-profile request_rate collapse from upstream load balancer misconfiguration
summary: request_rate on user-profile dropped to near zero for 25 minutes while the service itself stayed healthy.
root_cause: A load balancer health check was pointed at a path that a routine deploy removed, so the LB pulled every instance out of rotation.
evidence: request_rate floor with simultaneously falling cpu_usage; no ERROR logs from the service at all, which is the tell — a broken service logs errors, a starved one logs nothing.
resolution: Restored the health-check path and added a synthetic check on the LB target group.
lesson: Absence of traffic with absence of errors means the problem is upstream of the service, not inside it.

title: auth-service latency drift from unbounded session table growth
summary: Latency crept up roughly 3ms per hour over two days until the on-call noticed it had nearly doubled.
root_cause: The sessions table had no TTL cleanup job. A full table scan in the session lookup got progressively slower as rows accumulated.
evidence: WARN logs 'slow query detected (Nms) on table sessions' with N climbing steadily; latency ramp matched row-count growth almost exactly.
resolution: Added an index on the lookup column and a nightly TTL sweep.
lesson: Slow-query warnings whose duration is itself trending are the highest-signal evidence for a drift incident.

title: Correlated latency rise across all three services from noisy-neighbour host
summary: All three services showed a modest latency increase over the same 90-minute window without any deploy.
root_cause: An unrelated batch job was co-scheduled onto the same physical hosts and saturated local disk I/O.
evidence: Identical timing across three independent services; GC pause warnings on all three; no service-local cause in any of them.
resolution: Moved the batch job to a dedicated node pool and added anti-affinity rules.
lesson: When every service degrades together and none of them changed, look below the application at the shared substrate.

title: payment-gateway CPU spike from retry storm after transient downstream blip
summary: A three-minute downstream outage produced a 40-minute CPU spike that long outlasted the original fault.
root_cause: Unbounded retries with no jitter or circuit breaker. Once the downstream recovered, the accumulated retry backlog kept CPU pinned.
evidence: error_rate recovered well before cpu_usage did — the lag between the two is the retry-storm signature. ERROR logs 'retrying downstream call to billing-api, attempt N' with N reaching double digits.
resolution: Added exponential backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker at 50% error rate.
lesson: When CPU stays elevated after errors clear, suspect the retry policy rather than the original fault.

title: user-profile memory pressure surfacing as latency drift
summary: Latency drifted up over eight hours in a sawtooth pattern, resetting slightly after each GC cycle.
root_cause: An in-process LRU cache had its size bound removed in a refactor, so the heap grew until GC pressure dominated request time.
evidence: WARN logs 'GC pause Nms exceeded target' rising in both frequency and duration; the sawtooth shape distinguishes GC pressure from a pure resource leak.
resolution: Restored the cache bound and added a heap-utilisation alert.
lesson: Sawtooth latency drift with rising GC pauses is memory pressure; a smooth ramp is usually a leak or data growth.

title: auth-service error_rate rise from clock skew breaking token validation
summary: error_rate rose on auth-service and, an hour later, on user-profile, in both cases by only a few percentage points.
root_cause: NTP drifted on one host in the fleet. Tokens issued by that host looked not-yet-valid to peers, so validation failed intermittently and only for the fraction of traffic that host served.
evidence: The error rise was small because only one host in the pool was affected; the staggered onset across two services traced back to the same host being added to each pool at different times.
resolution: Fixed NTP and added clock-skew monitoring across the fleet.
lesson: A partial-magnitude error rise usually means a partial-fleet fault. Divide the observed rate by the affected host fraction before judging severity.

title: payment-gateway request_rate surge from client retry misconfiguration
summary: request_rate tripled for 20 minutes with a proportional CPU rise and no change in error_rate.
root_cause: A mobile client release shipped with a 1-second retry interval instead of 10 seconds.
evidence: cpu_usage tracked request_rate proportionally — the signature of genuine load rather than work-per-request regression. error_rate stayed flat because the service absorbed it.
resolution: Rate-limited by client version and shipped a client hotfix.
lesson: CPU rising in proportion to request_rate is load. CPU rising without it is a code or dependency regression.

title: Silent data-quality incident: user-profile served stale reads
summary: No metric moved outside its normal band, yet users reported stale profile data for six hours.
root_cause: A read replica stopped replicating. It stayed healthy and fast — it was just serving old data.
evidence: Nothing in cpu/latency/error/request_rate moved. Only replication lag, which was not being scraped, showed the fault.
resolution: Added replication-lag scraping and an alert at 30 seconds.
lesson: Not every incident is visible in the four golden signals. A clean detector run is not proof of health.

title: auth-service cascading failure from database failover
summary: A planned database failover took 90 seconds; the resulting error and latency spike lasted 25 minutes.
root_cause: Connection pools cached dead connections and did not probe liveness before handing them out, so every pooled connection had to fail once before being replaced.
evidence: ERROR logs 'failed to acquire database connection (Nms wait), aborting request' across two services sharing the same cluster; recovery was gradual rather than instant, tracking pool turnover.
resolution: Enabled pool liveness probes and reduced the max connection lifetime.
lesson: Recovery that is gradual rather than instant after a discrete event points at a cache or pool that has to age out.

title: False-positive storm from an untuned anomaly detector
summary: The on-call was paged 40 times in one night. Every page was noise from the diurnal traffic cycle.
root_cause: A z-score detector was fitted on a four-hour trailing window, which is shorter than the 24-hour diurnal period, so every morning ramp read as an anomaly.
evidence: Alert timestamps clustered at the same hour each day and correlated with request_rate, the driver of the cycle.
resolution: Extended the baseline to a full multiple of the diurnal period and added a seasonal term.
lesson: Alerts that recur at the same time of day are a modelling failure, not an incident. Check periodicity before investigating.

title: payment-gateway partial outage masked by aggregate metrics
summary: One of eight instances failed completely, but the service-level error_rate only moved from 0.4% to 3%.
root_cause: A disk filled on a single instance. It accepted connections and then failed every write.
evidence: Aggregate error_rate looked mild; per-instance breakdown showed one instance at 100% failure. ERROR logs from that instance dominated the window despite it serving one eighth of traffic.
resolution: Added disk-utilisation alerts and per-instance error-rate breakdown to the dashboard.
lesson: A small aggregate error rise can be a total failure of one shard. Always check whether errors are concentrated before sizing the impact.
